text: In December 1947, the first working transistor sat on a lab bench at Bell Labs. By 2018, by one estimate, we had made about thirteen sextillion of them: a thirteen with twenty-one zeros. That's more than any other thing people have ever made.

Here's where they are today. This is Apple's A-twenty Pro, from the iPhone eighteen Pro, made by TSMC on its two-nanometre process: the first iPhone chip with gate-all-around transistors. Zoom into a core, and you reach the view you work in every day: rows of standard cells, poly crossing diffusion.

And here's one transistor, in three-D. It's an illustrative nanosheet model from FET Lab, not the measured chip. Three sheets of silicon, five nanometres thick, carry the current from source to drain, and the gate wraps all the way around every one of them.

Every one of them has one job: let current through, or stop it. On. Off. This lecture is about how we got from the first one to this one, and why, every time we made it smaller, stopping the current turned out to be the hard part.

Five shapes: the planar transistor, the FinFET, the nanosheet, and two on the roadmap, the forksheet and the CFET. Each one answered a problem, of physics or of packing. Let's see why each one had to happen.
First: what the transistor replaced.

Before transistors, the switch was the vacuum tube: a hot cathode boiling off electrons, a grid that lets them through or turns them back, and a plate that collects them. ENIAC, in 1946, used about eighteen thousand of them, and some hundred and fifty kilowatts, and tubes kept burning out. Everyone wanted a cold, solid switch.

And the idea already existed. In 1925, Julius Lilienfeld patented a field-effect device: a metal plate over a thin film of semiconductor, insulated from it. Put a voltage on the plate, and it should pull charge into the film and change the current through it. That's a MOSFET, in everything but name.
On paper, the effect is big: the plate and the film are a capacitor, and ten volts should pull in plenty of charge. In practice, when Shockley tried it at Bell Labs in 1945, almost nothing happened.

John Bardeen worked out why: the surface. Where the crystal ends, there are broken bonds: states that trap the charge the gate induces, before it can reach the semiconductor. In our simple model, with a bare surface, only about two percent of that charge ends up in the semiconductor. The rest is stuck at the surface.
That was the dead end of the 1940s. So Bardeen and Brattain stopped fighting the surface, and started poking it.
December 1947. They were looking for amplification, on purpose.

On the sixteenth of December, it worked: two gold contacts pressed onto germanium, a hair's breadth apart, and the output was a bigger copy of the input. Not the field effect they were after: an unexpected mechanism, but real amplification. This is a replica of that first transistor, and its patent drawing.

Shockley's junction transistor followed in 1948. Electrons climb a hill to cross from emitter to collector, so the current is exponential in the base voltage: about sixty millivolts for ten times the current. Remember that sixty. It comes back.

But as a logic switch, a bipolar transistor needs base current just to stay on, so a chip full of them burns power standing still. The field effect needs almost no input current. It was still the better idea, if only the surface could be fixed.
The fix came from glass.

In the mid-1950s, at Bell Labs, Carl Frosch and Lincoln Derick found that silicon grows its own glass, silicon dioxide, and that it blocks dopants. Open a window in it, and you dope only there. Every mask layer you draw still works this way: open where you drew, blocked everywhere else.

Then Mohamed Atalla found something even more important: a carefully grown oxide also heals the surface. It ties up the broken bonds. In our model, the semiconductor's share of the charge goes from about two percent to about ninety-six. The gate can finally reach the silicon.

With the surface tamed, it all arrives at once: Kilby's integrated circuit in 1958; the planar process, and Noyce's planar chip, in 1959; and, in 1959 and '60, Atalla and Kahng's MOSFET: metal, oxide, semiconductor.

So how does a gate make a channel? Kahng's device was p-channel; we'll draw the n-channel mirror image, on p-type silicon. Raise the gate voltage, and the bands bend down at the surface. Past the threshold, the surface fills with electrons: an inverted layer, joining source to drain. That's the channel.

And the current is set by what you draw. In saturation, the square law: the drain current goes as W over L, times the overdrive squared. The ratio you draw sets the current, which is why matched devices copy W, L, fingers and orientation.

In 1963, Frank Wanlass paired an n and a p transistor: CMOS. With the input at either rail, one of them is off, so ideally no current flows from supply to ground, apart from leakage. Only while the input passes through the middle do both conduct, briefly. Most of the power goes into charging the load: alpha, C, V squared, f.
So by the mid-1960s we have it: a switch that barely leaks, spends power mostly when it switches, and is made by the billion, with masks and glass. So what happens if you draw everything smaller?
For the next forty years, the answer was: everything gets better.

In 1965, Gordon Moore plotted the number of components per chip, and saw it doubling every year. In 1975 he revised it to every two years. It isn't a law of physics. It's economics: the count at which each component is cheapest.

Start that two-year doubling from Intel's first microprocessor, the four-oh-oh-four, in 1971, with two thousand three hundred transistors. Our extrapolation lands near today's largest chips, like NVIDIA's B two-hundred: two dies, two hundred and eight billion transistors. Fifty years, on one line.

In 1974, Robert Dennard and his colleagues at IBM said how to do it. Shrink every dimension by a factor kappa: length, width, oxide. Shrink the voltage by kappa too. Then the electric fields inside stay the same, and the transistor behaves the same, only smaller.

Then every generation gives you twice the transistors in the same area, each one faster, and the same heat per square millimetre. That was the free lunch, and it's why your phone has billions of transistors and doesn't melt.
But look at Dennard's table again. Every row could keep shrinking for as long as we could draw smaller, except one: the voltage. Here's what that does.

This is Dennard's dial, one of the lecture's live labs. Shrink everything by about three generations. If the voltage shrank too, the power density would stay where it was. Here the voltage is stuck, and the clock still rises: the same patch of chip now runs about twenty-five times hotter per square millimetre. That's the problem of the next chapter.
Around 2005, something stopped. And a big part of the reason isn't engineering. It's thermodynamics.

Remember the hill from the junction transistor? Here it is for the MOSFET: electrons waiting in the source, and a barrier between them and the drain, whose height the gate sets. The current is the electrons that get over.

Here's the question that matters: when the switch is off, how many still get over? Those are your leakage. The electrons' energies have a Boltzmann tail, and the share above the barrier falls as e to the minus E over k T. Temperature sets it, not the designer.

So to get ten times as many over, you lower the barrier by k T times the natural log of ten: about sixty milli-electron-volts at room temperature. Another sixty: a hundred times. Every sixty is one decade of current.

One more piece: the gate pushes on the channel through the oxide, a capacitive divider, so the channel moves by only one over m of the gate voltage. Put them together, and you get the subthreshold swing. At room temperature, an ordinary transistor needs at least sixty millivolts of gate for each decade of current.

And here's the trap. To lower the supply and keep the on-current, you must lower the threshold, and every seventy millivolts or so off the threshold costs about ten times the leakage. Do that a few times, and the off current is no longer off. So the supply voltage stopped falling, near one volt.

You can see it in the clock speed. Base clocks rose about a thousandfold, then, around 2004, levelled off at three to four gigahertz. With the voltage stuck, a faster clock means more heat. So chips got more cores instead.

There was a second wall at the same time. The gate oxide was down to about one point two nanometres, a few atoms, and electrons tunnelled straight through it. The fix was hafnium oxide: a higher k, so a thicker layer gives the same grip, with far less tunnelling. Intel shipped it in 2007.
So by the mid-2000s, we had fixed the oxide. We could not fix Boltzmann. Here's the lab that shows it.

This is Boltzmann's fence. On the left, the hill, with the gate at zero point three volts and the barrier still a hundred and sixty milli-electron-volts high. On the right, the current against the gate voltage, on a log scale: at room temperature, with a perfect gate, it climbs one decade for every sixty millivolts; fifty-nine point five, to be exact. Cooling the chip makes the slope steeper, in this ideal model; a weaker grip makes it lazier.
Then the channel got short enough for the drain to join in.

Here's the hill again, drawn along the transistor: source on the left, drain on the right, gate on top. In a long channel, the gate holds the top of the hill. Put a voltage on the drain, and the drain end drops, but the top doesn't move. The gate is in charge.
Now shorten the channel. The source and the drain each bend the potential near them, and when they get close, their bends meet and pull the hill down by themselves. That's threshold roll-off.

And on a short channel, the drain voltage lowers the top of the barrier too. That's DIBL: drain-induced barrier lowering. The drain has become a second gate, one you don't control, and the leakage climbs.

The reason is a length, lambda: how far the source's and the drain's influence reaches into the channel. In our toy model, it depends on the channel's thickness, the oxide, and how many sides the gate holds. Long compared with lambda, the gate wins. Short, the drain wins. It all depends on L over lambda.

For analog, this has a direct price. If the drain moves the barrier, the drain voltage moves the current, so the output resistance falls, and with it the intrinsic gain, g m r o. That's one reason analog transistors are drawn longer than minimum.
So how do you get the grip back? Not by pushing the gate harder. Make lambda smaller: a thinner channel, and gate on more than one side. Here's the lab.

This is the barrier lab: a planar transistor with a thirty-nanometre gate, only about four and a half lambda long, and the drain at zero point seven five volts. The drain has reached in and pulled the hill down: about fifteen hundred times the leakage of a long channel. Wrap the gate around a thinner channel, as a FinFET does, and the same gate length is back in control.
If you can't put a gate under a flat channel, stand the channel up.

That's the fin: a thin wall of silicon standing on the wafer, gated from the sides. Hitachi showed one, called DELTA, in 1989. Berkeley's FinFET came in 1998 and '99. And in 2011, Intel announced its twenty-two-nanometre tri-gate transistors, in products the next year.

Cut it across, through the gate. The gate wraps over the top and down both sides of each fin: three faces instead of one. With a six-nanometre fin, lambda drops to a couple of nanometres. The grip is back.

So what's its width? Current flows from source to drain along the fin, on both sidewalls and the top, so each fin counts twice its height plus its width. Two fins, forty-five nanometres tall: a hundred and ninety-two nanometres.

But every fin is the same height, so the width comes in whole fins: ninety-six, a hundred and ninety-two, two hundred and eighty-eight nanometres, and nothing in between. In layout, you no longer draw W. You pick a number of fins, and a one-to-two mirror is two fins and four.
And the fin ran out of room: it's hard to make thinner, or taller. So turn it on its side, and slice it into sheets.

That's the nanosheet we started with: sheets of silicon five nanometres thick, with the gate all the way around each one, on four faces. Samsung started making them in 2022; TSMC's N two and Intel's eighteen A followed in 2025.
Each sheet counts all four faces. And here's the part layout people care about: the sheet width is set by the mask, not by a fin height. Width is something you draw again.

How do you put a gate under a sheet of silicon? You don't. You grow the space for it first: a stack of silicon and silicon-germanium, a few nanometres each. The silicon will be the channels. The silicon-germanium just holds the place.

Then a dummy gate, inner spacers, and the source and drain, grown from the sheets' ends, sitting on an insulator. Now the magic: pull out the dummy gate, dissolve the silicon-germanium, and the sheets hang in mid-air, held at their ends.

Coat everything with oxide and high-k, fill every gap with metal, and the gate wraps all the way around. That's one common route, and the idea at its heart: build the gate's space from a material you dissolve later.

So what stops the nanosheet? Look at the cell's height, set by the number of metal tracks. And inside it, the space between the n and the p sheets: here, forty-six nanometres, a third of the cell. It can't shrink much, because n and p need different gate metals, patterned apart.

One answer, on imec's roadmap: the forksheet. Put a thin insulating wall between n and p, and push the sheets right against it. In these schematic models, the cell gets about a fifth shorter. imec's 2021 forksheets switched about as well as nanosheets, and the version on the roadmap puts the wall at the cell's edge.
Or remove the space completely, by building upward.

The CFET, the complementary FET, stacks the n transistor right on top of the p. Cut across the gate: two sheets below, two above, and, in this model, one gate around all four. Two transistors, one footprint. It's on imec's roadmap for the early 2030s.

Line up the four inverter cells at one scale, rail to rail: a hundred and fifty-six, a hundred and thirty-six, a hundred and six, and seventy-four nanometres, in these schematic models. Each step took the n-to-p space away, and the cell got shorter.

Look where the CFET's power rails went: to the back of the wafer, where they can be thick, so less voltage is lost on the way. That doesn't wait for the CFET: Intel already ships backside power with nanosheets, in eighteen A.

And stacking stacks the heat: up to twice the power per area, depending on the workload. With the heat sink below the wafer, the upper tier's heat has the longer way out. Here's how the cells compare when you build them.

This lab builds an inverter cell to scale, on a twenty-four-nanometre metal pitch. With two fins per transistor, the cell needs seven tracks; with nanosheets, six; with a forksheet's wall, five. Here's the CFET: n stacked on p, it needs just seventy-four nanometres, and fits in four tracks. These are schematic models with FET Lab's spacings, not a foundry's rules.

And here's FET Lab's three-D model of a monolithic CFET, cut through the gate: the p transistor's two sheets below, the n transistor's two above, each wrapped in oxide, high-k and metal, inside one gate. In the live deck, you can turn it, cut it, and peel the layers away.
From here on, it's research.

Research now: channels just a few atoms thick, like molybdenum disulfide, with no surface to roughen. imec's roadmap brings them in around the 2040s. And their catch is the contacts, where Bardeen's old surface states come back.

And switches that try to beat sixty millivolts per decade, by tunnelling through the barrier instead of climbing over it. Tunnel transistors have done it in the lab, and in 2024 a team at MIT did it while still carrying useful current.

So here's what I'd like you to take away. Every smaller transistor in this story had to do three things at once: turn off; still turn on, with enough current; and fit into a cell you can build by the billion. The off state is the thread that kept coming back.

And through all of it, k T over q, times the natural log of ten, fifty-nine point five millivolts per decade, is still the best an ordinary transistor can do at room temperature. Lab devices have crossed it. Making them useful and reliable, by the billion, is the next chapter.
Thank you for watching.
